items.value: Neither statement is correct — both invert the real distinction between jagirdars and zamindars
items.reasoning: Statement 1 misdescribes both offices: a jagir was a revenue assignment made to a mansabdar in lieu of cash salary for MILITARY and administrative service (maintaining a contingent of troops), not for judicial and police duties; and zamindars were not free of obligations, being expected to assist in maintaining law and order and to supply men when required. Statement 2 reverses the true position: jagirs were transferable and non-hereditary, with jagirdars routinely shifted from one assignment to another precisely to stop them striking roots, while zamindari revenue rights were hereditary and saleable. Both statements being wrong, the answer is neither.

items.value: Ceiling laws took the family, not the individual, as the unit of holding
items.reasoning: The National Guidelines of 1972 fixed the ceiling on the FAMILY as the operative unit (typically a family of five), precisely because the earlier individual-based ceilings had been defeated by partitions and benami transfers, so A states the settled design of ceiling legislation. B is wrong because the stated aims of land reform were abolition of intermediaries, tenancy reform, ceilings and consolidation — supplying land to every landless household was never achievable nor the declared major aim. C is wrong: land reform is not what made cash crops predominant, and they are not predominant. D is plainly wrong, since ceiling laws carried extensive exemptions — plantations of tea, coffee and rubber, orchards, cooperative farms, religious and charitable trusts.

items.value: The World Economic Forum publishes the Global Competitiveness Report
items.reasoning: The Global Competitiveness Report, with its Global Competitiveness Index, is a flagship publication of the World Economic Forum (Geneva). The IMF publishes the World Economic Outlook, UNCTAD the World Investment Report and Trade and Development Report, and the World Bank the World Development Report and the erstwhile Doing Business report.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 only — the monopoly ended except for tea and China, and Crown sovereignty was asserted
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is textbook correct: the Charter Act of 1813 threw Indian trade open to all British subjects but preserved the Company's monopoly of the tea trade and of trade with China. Statement 2 is also a standard feature of the Act — it expressly asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the territories held by the Company. Statement 3 overstates the Act: control of Indian revenues had already been vested in the Board of Control by Pitt's India Act of 1784, and the 1813 Act only required the Company to keep its commercial and territorial accounts separate, which is not the same as Parliament taking control of Indian revenues. RUNNER-UP: D (all three). D would win if the examiner treats the 1813 Act's separation of territorial accounts and its regulation of the Company's dividend and surplus as amounting to Parliamentary control of Indian revenues; the item pivots entirely on how generously statement 3 is read, since statements 1 and 2 are beyond dispute and no option lets either of them be false.

items.value: Both — Swadeshi revived indigenous crafts and industries, and the National Council of Education was a part of it
items.reasoning: The Swadeshi Movement launched after the 1905 partition of Bengal deliberately promoted indigenous enterprise — handloom weaving, textile mills, soap and match factories, tanneries, national banks and insurance — so statement 1 is correct. The National Council of Education was founded on 15 August 1906 as the national-education limb of the same movement, and it set up the Bengal National College with Aurobindo Ghosh as principal, so statement 2 is correct too.

items.value: All three pairs are correctly matched
items.reasoning: The All India Anti-Untouchability League was founded by Mahatma Gandhi in September 1932 after the Poona Pact and was later renamed the Harijan Sevak Sangh. The All India Kisan Sabha was formed at Lucknow in 1936 with Swami Sahajanand Saraswati as its first president. The Self-Respect Movement was launched in 1925 in the Madras Presidency by E. V. Ramaswami Naicker, Periyar. All three pairings hold.

items.value: Sohgaura is not a Harappan site
items.reasoning: Sohgaura lies in Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh and is known for the Sohgaura copper-plate inscription of the Mauryan period, which records famine-relief storehouses; it has nothing to do with the Harappan civilisation. Chanhudaro and Kot Diji are Harappan sites in Sindh and Desalpur is a Harappan site in Kachchh, Gujarat.

items.value: Kanganahalli, where a relief panel labelled Ranyo Asoko carries a portrait of Ashoka
items.reasoning: Excavations at the Kanganahalli stupa near Sannati in Karnataka uncovered a relief sculpture of a king with attendants inscribed in Brahmi as Ranyo Asoko, that is King Ashoka — the only known contemporaneous stone portrait of Ashoka identified by name. Shahbazgarhi carries a Major Rock Edict in Kharoshthi but no portrait, and Sohgaura's copper plate and Sanchi's gateways carry no such labelled portrait.

items.value: All three — deification of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva path, and image worship with ritual
items.reasoning: Mahayana Buddhism transformed the Buddha from a human teacher into a transcendent, divine being to be worshipped, so 1 holds. It made the Bodhisattva ideal, the aspirant who defers nirvana to help all beings, central in place of the arhat ideal, so 2 holds. And it embraced the making and worship of Buddha images along with devotional ritual, in contrast with the earlier aniconic tradition, so 3 holds.

items.value: Vishti was treated as a source of state income — a tax rendered by the people in the form of labour
items.reasoning: In Gupta-period sources vishti appears as an exaction owed to the state, a levy discharged in labour rather than in cash or kind, and it is listed alongside other dues in grants that transfer it to donees; that is exactly what A states. B is wrong because vishti is attested in inscriptions from central India and from Kathiawar, so it was not absent from those regions. C is wrong because vishti was unpaid, which is what made it forced. D is an invention: there was no rule sending the eldest son.

items.value: Vijayanagara temple architecture
items.reasoning: The kalyana mandapa, a pillared marriage hall built to house the ritual wedding of the deity and consort, is a distinctive addition of Vijayanagara temple complexes, alongside the amman shrine, the hundred-pillared hall and towering gopurams — seen at Vitthala and Hazara Rama at Hampi and at Vellore and Kanchipuram. Chalukya, Chandela and Rashtrakuta temple building shows no such feature.

items.value: Statement 1 only — the Amil was the revenue collector
items.reasoning: Amil was indeed the official charged with collecting land revenue in the Delhi Sultanate, so 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the iqta was a West Asian institution of the Islamic world, brought to India by the Turks, not an ancient indigenous one. Statement 3 is wrong on both the office and the dynasty: Mir Bakshi was a Mughal office, head of the military department under Akbar, whereas the corresponding Sultanate officer was the Ariz-i-Mumalik.

items.value: Neither — both statements are chronologically impossible
items.reasoning: Nimbarka, founder of the Dvaitadvaita school and of the Nimbarka Sampradaya, belongs to roughly the twelfth to thirteenth century, some three or four hundred years before Akbar, so statement 1 fails. Statement 2 fails the other way: Kabir belongs to the fifteenth century while Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi lived from 1564 to 1624, so the later figure cannot have influenced the earlier one.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — Gandhi drove the abolition of indenture, and Congress was outlawed after the salt satyagraha
items.reasoning: Gandhi's sustained campaign against the export of Indian indentured labour led to the system being ended in 1917, so 1 is correct. Statement 2 is the reverse of what happened: at Lord Chelmsford's Delhi War Conference in April 1918 Gandhi supported the recruitment resolution, speaking briefly in Hindustani in its favour, and afterwards worked as a recruiter in Kheda. Statement 3 is correct: following the breach of the salt law in 1930 the colonial government declared the Congress organisation unlawful and arrested its leadership.

items.value: All three pairs are correctly matched
items.reasoning: Sir Tej Bahadur Sapru was a leading Moderate who presided over the All India Liberal Federation, the National Liberal Federation formed by those who left the Congress in 1918. K. C. Neogy was a member of the Constituent Assembly and went on to chair the First Finance Commission. P. C. Joshi was General Secretary of the Communist Party of India from 1935 to 1947. Every pairing stands.

items.value: The claim that Akbar gave him the title Tansen is the incorrect one — Akbar conferred Mian, not Tansen
items.reasoning: Born Ramtanu Pandey, he was already styled Tansen at the court of Rewa and it was Akbar who honoured him with the title Mian, giving the familiar form Mian Tansen; so A is the statement that is not correct. The other three are true: he composed dhrupads addressed to Hindu deities, he composed pieces in praise of his patrons, and he is credited with new ragas including Miyan ki Malhar, Miyan ki Todi and Darbari Kanada.

items.value: Jahangir
items.reasoning: Akbar's atelier was organised around large illustrated manuscripts such as the Hamzanama, Razmnama and Akbarnama. Jahangir, whose personal taste ran to naturalism and connoisseurship, redirected the studio towards single-page paintings mounted in muraqqa albums, above all individual portraiture and studies of birds, animals and flowers. Shah Jahan continued the album tradition rather than initiating the shift.

items.value: Valley of Flowers National Park
items.reasoning: The Valley of Flowers in Uttarakhand lies wholly above roughly 3,200 metres, well above the tree line, so the whole park is in the temperate-alpine belt. Manas sits in the Bhabar and terai lowlands of Assam and is tropical. Namdapha runs from about 200 metres to over 4,500 metres and so spans tropical, subtropical, temperate and alpine zones rather than lying completely in one. Neora Valley likewise starts near 180 metres in the subtropical foothills.

items.value: NITI Aayog
items.reasoning: The Atal Innovation Mission, which runs the Atal Tinkering Labs and Atal Incubation Centres, was established as a flagship initiative under NITI Aayog to promote a culture of innovation and entrepreneurship. It is not housed in the Department of Science and Technology, the Ministry of Labour and Employment, or the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship.

items.value: At the Arctic Circle the Sun does not set below the horizon on 21 June
items.reasoning: 21 June is the summer solstice for the northern hemisphere, when the Sun is vertically overhead at the Tropic of Cancer and the entire area from the Arctic Circle to the North Pole has twenty-four hours of daylight, so at the Arctic Circle the Sun does not set. B is the opposite case, since the Antarctic Circle is then in continuous darkness. C describes the equinoxes of 21 March and 23 September, and D describes 22 December.

items.value: Tobacco, cocoa and rubber — all three were domesticated in the Americas
items.reasoning: Tobacco was domesticated in the Americas, cacao in Mesoamerica and the upper Amazon, and the rubber tree Hevea brasiliensis in Amazonia; all three reached the Old World only after 1492, so A is a clean New World set. B fails because cotton was independently domesticated in the Old World as well, with Gossypium arboreum and G. herbaceum indigenous to Asia and Africa. C and D fail outright because coffee is Ethiopian, sugarcane is from New Guinea and Southeast Asia, and wheat is from the Fertile Crescent.

items.value: Statement 1 only — the Asiatic lion alone is found in the wild in India and nowhere else
items.reasoning: The only surviving wild population of the Asiatic lion is in the Gir landscape of Gujarat, so 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong: the double-humped Bactrian camel occurs naturally across Central Asia, with wild herds in the Gobi of Mongolia and China, India's population in Nubra being only a small part of its range. Statement 3 is wrong because the great one-horned rhinoceros is also found naturally in Nepal, notably in Chitwan, besides its Indian populations in Assam and north Bengal.

items.value: Pairs 1 and 2 only — Hampi stands on the Tungabhadra, not the Malaprabha
items.reasoning: At Pandharpur the Bhima river takes a crescent bend and is locally called the Chandrabhaga, on whose bank the Vitthala temple stands, so pair 1 is right. Tiruchirappalli lies on the Cauvery, with Srirangam on the island between the Cauvery and the Coleroon, so pair 2 is right. Pair 3 is wrong: Hampi, the Vijayanagara capital, lies on the Tungabhadra; the Malaprabha is the river of the Chalukyan sites of Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal.

items.value: Because price levels differ from State to State
items.reasoning: India's official poverty lines are state-specific and separately fixed for rural and urban areas because they are anchored to a consumption basket valued at local prices; where prices are higher, the money value of the same basket is higher, so the line itself is higher. The poverty RATE and the Gross State Product are outcomes measured against the line rather than inputs into fixing it, and the quality of the public distribution system does not enter the computation of the line.

items.value: Reducing global warming — both are proposed geoengineering techniques
items.reasoning: Both measures are climate-engineering proposals aimed at the planet's radiation balance. Injecting sulphate aerosols into the stratosphere is solar radiation management, mimicking the cooling that follows a large volcanic eruption by reflecting incoming sunlight. Cirrus cloud thinning works on the other side of the budget, seeding high cirrus so that they trap less outgoing longwave radiation. Neither is a rain-making, cyclone-suppression or solar-wind technique.
